entries.lesson_core_move: Set up the one-sided Laplace transform as $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, identifying the lower limit, exponential weighting, and complex $s$-domain representation used for causal signal and system analysis.

sections.section_title: Introduction to One-Sided Laplace Transform Definition

blocks.text: In causal signal and system analysis, we start from right-sided behavior, so the one-sided Laplace transform is the direct map used when signals and inputs are modeled on $t \ge 0^-$ rather than on the entire real line.
The complex frequency variable is written as $s=\sigma+j\omega$, and it is the independent frequency-domain coordinate that the time signal $x(t)$ is converted into.

The one-sided definition is $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$: we identify the time-domain signal $x(t)$, the exponential kernel $e^{-st}$, and the differential element $dt$ before evaluating anything.
Use $0^-$, not just $0$, so behavior at the origin is included correctly (such as impulses or jumps) while preserving the causal setup used for initial conditions.

Compared with the bilateral definition, the one-sided transform uses lower limit $0^-$ as its domain anchor, then keeps the same kernel and complex variable $s$, so the structural difference is the causal interval choice.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Time-Domain Signal and $s$-Domain Transform

example_content.example_prompt: Write the one-sided Laplace setup for $x(t)=u(t)$ and identify the corresponding $X(s)$ setup notation.

explanation_blocks.text: For this worked example, identify the time-domain signal from the prompt and map it directly into the one-sided transform definition; the move is recognition first, setup second, no integration yet.
The cue is $x(t)=u(t)$, which is causal by definition, so the target one-sided form still uses the same lower limit $0^-$ used in the section core move.

That expression is the required output: the time-domain signal is now written as $u(t)$, the weighting term is $e^{-st}$, and the differential is over $dt$ from $0^-$ to $\infty$; this preserves the causal one-sided transform setup for later evaluation and for the upcoming multiple-choice practice.

sections.section_title: Setting the One-Sided Integration Limits

example_content.example_prompt: Set the integral limits for $X(s)$ when $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and show why the lower limit is written $0^-$.

explanation_blocks.text: The goal is to choose the one-sided integration interval before any algebraic simplification: the signal is causal and the transform setup must therefore keep the causal lower bound.
From the prompt, identify the cue $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which is nonzero only for $t \ge 0$, so the time-domain support implies the one-sided interval rule $t \ge 0^-$.
Substitute $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ into the definition and keep both $0^-$ and the exponential weighting unchanged in place.

Write the final result as $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} e^{-2t}u(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. The $0^-$ lower limit is required so behavior at the origin is included in the causal convention used by the one-sided transform.

sections.section_title: Applying the Exponential Weighting Factor

example_content.example_prompt: Write the one-sided integral for $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$ showing the weighted integrand $x(t)e^{-st}$ clearly.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue now is $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$, and the task is to apply the one-sided rule from earlier with the exponential weighting term explicit.
Substitute $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$ directly into the template and multiply by the kernel $e^{-st}$.
Combine exponentials to make the weighted integrand explicit before integration: $3e^{-t}e^{-st}=3e^{-(s+1)t}$, so the setup is $3u(t)e^{-(s+1)t}$ inside the one-sided integral.
The final weighted-setup result is $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} 3e^{-(s+1)t}u(t)\,dt$, with bounds unchanged at $0^-$ and $\infty$.

sections.section_title: Writing the Complete One-Sided Laplace Transform Setup

example_content.example_prompt: Write the complete one-sided Laplace definition for $x(t)=u(t)$ as a final setup expression.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the target form in the required order: signal, kernel, and integral bounds in one line.
Substitute the signal $x(t)=u(t)$ from the cue and keep the same causal interval $0^-\le t < \infty$.
Verify there is no missing kernel term, no wrong integral limit, and no dropped one-sided qualifier: all three must appear together in the final template.
Final setup (correct form): $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} u(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. A common confusion is using bilateral bounds, omitting $0^-$, or writing only $e^{-t}$ without the full $e^{-st}$ weight.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the $0^-$ convention when setting up one-sided Laplace transforms so discontinuities and impulses at $t=0$ are included consistently in causal signal analysis.

sections.section_title: Introduction to The $0^-$ Convention

blocks.text: A one-sided Laplace transform step is a setup move for causal signals, so the target here is to define the integral format before any solving starts. The core move is to carry the origin convention explicitly so later examples treat discontinuities and impulses at $0$ consistently.
Use the interval choice $0^- \\le t < \\infty$ as the integration domain: for section work in this module, this is the signal-notation object that declares a causal transform setup.
With the base case $x(t)=u(t)$, the setup starts at $0^-$ so all causal support is included, including any jump or impulse behavior at the origin, while support for $t<0$ is excluded by definition.
Section rule: write $X(s)=\\int_{0^-}^{\\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\\,dt$ first, then substitute $x(t)$; this is the format to reuse in every later example before applying the rest of the Laplace machinery.

sections.section_title: Setting a One-Sided Laplace Integral from $0^-$

example_content.example_prompt: Write the one-sided setup for $x(t)=u(t)+2u(t-1)$ and keep the transform expression in the form of a causal integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a causal signal written as a step sum: $x(t)=u(t)+2u(t-1)$. The action is to encode this signal in the one-sided template directly, so the setup stays symbolic and preserves the lower limit convention before any integration is done.
Use the one-sided rule for this module: for any causal setup, write $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ first, then place $x(t)$ and keep the same bound for every causal branch.

Decompose the cue into its pieces and substitute it into the template: $u(t)$ contributes over $[0^-,\infty)$ and $2u(t-1)$ is a delayed causal branch that is still inserted into the same $0^-$ setup without changing the lower limit.

Result: the final setup is notation-complete when it is expressed as a causal one-sided integral with $0^-$ explicitly present and the delayed step left as the same causal form; evaluation and simplification come later.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Signals That Change at $t=0$

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=\begin{cases}5,&t<0\\0,&0\le t<1\\2,&t\ge 1\end{cases}$, write the one-sided setup and identify which branch is included.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the piecewise signal $x(t)$, so the first move is to mark which branches are active for each interval and then keep only the causal interval from the one-sided rule.
Apply the same causal template used in previous sections: $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. The lower bound remains $0^-$ and the integration only uses causal support.

Since $x(t)=5$ for $t<0$, that branch is excluded by causality. On $[0,1)$ the branch is $0$, and for $t\ge 1$ the branch is $2$, so the causal setup can be written as the retained post-origin branch only.

Result rule to carry forward: bounded jumps at $t=0$ do not add a finite-area term in the integral setup; only the interval starting at $0^-$ is kept and only causal branches contribute, with impulses handled separately by a distribution rule.

sections.section_title: Including an Impulse at $t=0$

example_content.example_prompt: Find the one-sided Laplace setup and final transform expression for $x(t)=2\delta(t)+u(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a mixed signal with an origin impulse and a causal step: $x(t)=2\delta(t)+u(t)$. The first action is to set the one-sided template exactly once, then separate the impulse and step parts.
Use the same causal rule from earlier sections: $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. Keep this form first, then substitute the mixed signal into it.

Split the setup into two terms and apply the origin rule for the $\delta$ contribution. The distribution term is supported at the lower endpoint, so $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}2\delta(t)e^{-st}\,dt=2$ under this convention.
The finite-jump rule from the previous section still applies separately: bounded jumps do not produce finite-area terms, but the impulse term does produce a constant contribution from the endpoint.
Result: keep this as the final setup-expression form with one-sided lower limit and explicit impulse constant, then let later steps simplify the remaining one-sided step integral if needed.

sections.section_title: Excluding Signal Behavior Before $t=0$

example_content.example_prompt: Write the one-sided setup for $x(t)=\begin{cases}3,&t<0\\t^2,&t\ge 0\end{cases}$ and state the excluded pre-origin branch.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a piecewise signal with one noncausal branch and one causal branch. First separate support regions so that only post-origin content can survive the one-sided setup.
Apply the template from this topic: $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. Keep $0^-$ fixed as the lower endpoint and enforce causality before writing any value changes.

Result: the excluded pre-origin branch is $x(t)=3$ for $t<0$, and the retained branch is $x(t)=t^2$ on $t\ge0$. This gives the compact direct-expression form used by the next question model: $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}t^2e^{-st}\,dt$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of $e^{-at}u(t)$ from the $0^-$-to-$\infty$ definition, producing $X(s)=1/(s+a)$ with convergence condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$ as the base exponential transform pair.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Laplace Transform of $e^{-at}u(t)$

blocks.text: The target move is to identify the one-sided transform setup for $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$ and turn it into a reusable exponential transform pair.

Use the base cue as the causal exponential step: in this topic, $u(t)$ is the on-off switch that is $1$ for $t\ge0$ and $0$ for $t<0$, so the one-sided transform uses the interval from $0^-$ to infinity.
Drop $u(t)$ inside the interval $t\ge0$ by substitution and combine exponents into one weighted exponential: $e^{-(s+a)t}$.
This section stops here with setup; next sections evaluate the integral to get $1/(s+a)$ and then state the convergence condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$ before extending to named examples.

sections.section_title: Setting Up the One-Sided Integral for $e^{-at}u(t)$

example_content.example_prompt: Set up the one-sided Laplace transform integral for $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, including all limits and factors.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the one-sided definition as the cue for this step: for any signal $x(t)$, the transform setup is $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{x(t)\}=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$.
Apply that rule to the specific cue $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ by substituting the signal into the template.
Because this is one-sided, keep the lower limit at $0^-$ and keep the $u(t)$ factor visible, so the causal-support rule is explicit before any integral evaluation.
This is the complete setup for the next section: the concrete case $a=3$ is now written with correct limits and one-sided notation.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Integral to Obtain $1/(s+a)$

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-2t}u(t)\}$ from the one-sided integral and simplify the result.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the one-sided setup from the previous section as the cue: evaluate the setup for the concrete signal $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ as a definite integral, not another setup.
Recognize the integrand as an exponential and use the antiderivative rule for $\int e^{-(s+2)t}dt$.
Apply bounds from $0^-$ to $\infty$ and require $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-2$ so the upper limit term decays.
So the worked result is $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-2t}u(t)\}=1/(s+2)$, which confirms the target base-pair form for the same canonical family.

sections.section_title: Determining the Convergence Condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$

example_content.example_prompt: Determine the ROC for $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-at}u(t)\}=\frac{1}{s+a}$ by using the limit behavior at infinity.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the antiderivative boundary form from the previous step as the cue, now read as a condition check rather than another algebraic manipulation.
A finite one-sided transform requires the upper-limit term to vanish, so evaluate $\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-(s+a)t}$.
Convert that inequality to the ROC statement in terms of $s$ by subtracting $\operatorname{Re}(a)=a$ (assuming real $a$ in this topic convention).
Therefore the final transform statement is $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-at}u(t)\}=\frac{1}{s+a},\;\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$.

sections.section_title: Reading Specific Exponential Signals as $1/(s+a)$ Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: Write the transform pair for $e^{-5t}u(t)$ and list its ROC.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the base-pair template as the cue: for a signal of the form $e^{-at}u(t)$, the transform is $1/(s+a)$ with the associated one-sided ROC.
Match $e^{-5t}u(t)$ directly to the template and identify $a=5$.
The final result is a quick recognition move: parameter substitution into the shared template and ROC transfer, not a re-derivation.

entries.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the one-sided Laplace transform of $u(t)$ as $U(s)=1/s$ by treating it as the $a=0$ case of $e^{-at}u(t)$ and checking the $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$ convergence condition.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Introduction to Laplace Transform of the Unit Step

blocks.text: The target object in this step is the one-sided Laplace transform of the unit step. You should recognize that $u(t)$ is the special case of $e^{-at}u(t)$ when $a=0$, so this section reuses the same transform structure from the previous lesson and narrows it to the simplest base signal.

Write the one-sided transform setup directly from the definition: start with the time-domain signal, attach the exponential kernel, and keep the $0^-$ lower limit so the setup is valid for causal signals in one-sided Laplace notation.
Because $u(t)=1$ for $t\ge 0$, the integral reduces to a plain exponential integral over the one-sided interval.

Integrate once to get $U(s)=\left[-\frac{1}{s}e^{-st}\right]_{0^-}^{\infty}=\frac{1}{s}$, and then require the convergence condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$ so the upper-limit term vanishes. This gives the unit-step pair result, which we will reuse throughout later examples in this lesson.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Computing the Unit Step Transform as the $a=0$ Exponential Case

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of $x(t)=u(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The key cue is that this is the same one-sided exponential-pattern transform from the previous section, with the new wrinkle $a=0$. Use the standard causal definition and write the transform directly from the signal.
For $t\ge 0$, $u(t)=1$. Replace the signal with that constant and simplify the setup to an exponential-only integral over the one-sided interval.
Integrate, then evaluate the antiderivative at the bounds.
Require $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$ so the term $e^{-sb}$ decays to zero as $b\to\infty$, leaving only $\frac{1}{s}$.
State the transform pair as $u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{s}$, and note that this is explicitly a one-sided result with lower limit $0^-$ because we are using the unilateral definition.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Deriving $U(s)=1/s$ from the One-Sided Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $\int_{0^-}^{\infty} e^{-st}\,dt$ and obtain the one-sided transform $U(s)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use this as a bound-checking verification pass. The cue is still the unit-step transform, but now the goal is to make the one-sided limit handling explicit so it can be reproduced step by step.
Since $u(t)$ is one on $t\ge 0$, the integral is the same as evaluating the antiderivative of $e^{-st}=e^{-(s+0)t}$, with the lower limit kept as $0^-$.
Evaluate the lower bound first: at $t\to 0^-$, $\lim_{t\to 0^-}e^{-st}=1$, so the lower-term contribution is $-(-1/s\cdot 1)=1/s$.
Now evaluate the upper bound with a parameter $b$ to isolate convergence: write $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}e^{-st}\,dt=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left(-\frac{1}{s}e^{-sb}\right)+\frac{1}{s}$.

For convergence the first term must vanish; this happens only when $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$. If $\operatorname{Re}(s)\le 0$, the upper expression does not decay and the one-sided integral does not produce a finite transform.
Write the final reusable statement as $u(t)\leftrightarrow 1/s$ with explicit ROC tag $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$, which is the form students will reuse directly in the next practice question model.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Checking the $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$ Convergence Condition

example_content.example_prompt: For $U(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} e^{-st}\,dt$, determine where the integral converges.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a convergence check rather than a new integration. Keep the same expression from the previous step and test when the upper-limit term decays.
Substitute into the exponential to isolate decay: $e^{-st}=e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}$. Only $e^{-\sigma t}$ controls the magnitude as $t\to\infty$.

Evaluate the limit at infinity: if $\sigma>0$, then $\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\sigma t}=0$ and the improper integral term vanishes. If $\sigma\le 0$, the term does not decay, so the one-sided integral is not finite.
State the region of convergence as a required part of the pair knowledge, not a decoration: $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$, i.e. $\sigma>0$.
Carry this forward by attaching the same condition to the stored pair $u(t)\leftrightarrow 1/s$, so later inverse lookup and inverse-check questions remain mathematically valid.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Recognizing $1/s$ as the Unit Step Transform Pair

example_content.example_prompt: Match $U(s)=1/s$, $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$, to its one-sided time-domain signal and explain the match.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is inversion-retrieval: use the computed $U(s)$ and convert it back to the time-domain signal family from this lesson, keeping the ROC as part of the answer.
Start from nearby causal pairs in this sequence: $\mathcal{L}\{u(t)\}=1/s$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$, and $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-at}u(t)\}=1/(s+a)$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$.
Reject nonmatching forms by checking the denominator pattern and ROC. A shifted exponential like $1/(s+1)$ is not $1/s$, and missing or opposite-sided ROC also disqualifies the exact unit-step match.
The exact pair is therefore

Record this as a reusable inverse rule: $\frac{1}{s}$ with right-half-plane ROC is the causal unit step, while $\operatorname{Re}(s)$ tag errors (for example $\operatorname{Re}(s)<0$) should be flagged before selecting an answer.

entries.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of $\delta(t)$ by using the $0^-$ convention to include the impulse at the origin and convert it into the constant $s$-domain value $1$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Introduction to Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse

blocks.text: Use the one-sided definition as your starting template: $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{x(t)\}=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, where the integral starts at $0^-$ rather than $0$.

For impulse calculations, the key cue is the sifting identity: the integral of $\delta(t)$ against a test function returns the function value at zero, and the $0^-$ lower limit keeps this rule aligned with one-sided causal setup.
Apply the sifting step directly: $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}\delta(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ collapses to $e^{-s\cdot 0}$, because the sampled point is $t=0$.
So this section’s result is $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}=1$, and keeping $0^-$ is the boundary rule that preserves origin impulses in later shifted-impulse and signal-composition steps.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Applying Sifting to the One-Sided Transform of $\delta(t)$

example_content.example_prompt: Find $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The goal here is to compute a concrete one-sided impulse transform by direct substitution, starting from the definition of the operation and then applying the sifting rule at the impulse location.
Now recognize the cue: this is an impulse multiplied by a smooth test function, so use sifting. With $f(t)=e^{-st}$, the term $\delta(t)f(t)$ evaluates to $f(0)$ inside the one-sided interval.
Since the lower limit is $0^-$, the origin impulse is included in the one-sided interval, so this sampled value is retained. Simplify to $1$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Including the Origin Impulse with the $0^-$ Lower Limit

example_content.example_prompt: Show why using $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}$ keeps $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}=1$, while $\int_{0^+}^{\infty}$ would omit the origin impulse.

explanation_blocks.text: Use both one-sided candidates so the boundary rule is explicit before evaluating the transform value.
For one-sided transforms, the convention rule is: use the lower limit $0^-$ when an impulse or jump at the origin must be included in the signal interval.
Only the $0^-$ interval samples the boundary impulse at $t=0$, so it returns the sifting contribution; the $0^+$ interval starts strictly after the impulse and contributes $0$.
This topic’s core convention is therefore operational: with one-sided transforms, include the origin impulse via $0^-$ so that $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}=1$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Transforming Scaled Unit Impulses at the Origin

example_content.example_prompt: Find $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{5\delta(t)\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: This is the same one-sided impulse setup as before, now with an amplitude coefficient: treat $x(t)=5\delta(t)$ and keep the $0^-$ lower limit convention.
Use the sifting rule and pull out the constant $5$ from the integral, since constants are linear under integration.
Apply the same impulse-at-the-origin evaluation as earlier: $\delta(t)$ samples $e^{-st}$ at $t=0$ and the lower limit includes the boundary value.
Therefore, $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{5\delta(t)\}=5\cdot 1 =5$, and the same pattern is $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{A\delta(t)\}=A$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a shifted impulse lies inside the $0^-$-to-$\infty$ one-sided interval, then use sifting to convert $A\delta(t-T)$ into $Ae^{-sT}$ for $T\ge 0$.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Laplace Transform of Shifted Impulses

blocks.text: The shifted-impulse lesson starts from a fixed rule: for one-sided Laplace work, first test whether the signal event lies in the interval $0^- \le t < \infty$, then apply the sifting rule with that support check.
Every one-sided transform begins with the definition

Now use the same definition with $x(t)=A\delta(t-T)$. The impulse contributes only at the single time $t=T$, so evaluate the integrand there. This gives $\mathcal{L}\{A\delta(t-T)\}=A e^{-sT}$ when $T$ is inside the one-sided interval.

Use this as a two-step execution check in every example: identify $T$, verify whether it satisfies $T\ge 0$, then write $Ae^{-sT}$ with the same amplitude and exponential term from the impulse location.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Shifted Impulse Inside the One-Sided Interval

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{3\delta(t-2)\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue that this is a shifted impulse in the form $A\delta(t-T)$, then identify the parameters directly: $A=3$ and $T=2$.
Start from the one-sided definition for the input signal
Substitute $x(t)=3\delta(t-2)$ and keep the same lower limit.
Apply sifting at $t=2$: the impulse picks the integrand at $t=2$, giving $3e^{-2s}$. Since $2\ge 0$, the impulse is inside the one-sided interval and the result is kept.
So the final transform is $3e^{-2s}$, with the amplitude and shift preserved from the original impulse.

sections.section_title: Including Amplitude in a Shifted Impulse Transform

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{-\frac{5}{2}\delta(t-3)\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: This is the same shifted-impulse cue as before, but now the new wrinkle is a signed fractional amplitude: $x(t)=-\frac{5}{2}\delta(t-3)$. The rule is still $A\delta(t-T)\to Ae^{-sT}$ with $T\ge 0$.
Write the one-sided definition for this signal first.
Substitute $x(t)=-\frac{5}{2}\delta(t-3)$ into the definition.
Apply sifting at $t=3$. The scalar amplitude is preserved and multiplies the kernel value, so $e^{-s(3)}$ is attached to $-\frac{5}{2}$. Check the support rule: $T=3\ge 0$, so this term is included.
The final transform is $-\frac{5}{2}e^{-3s}$, with the coefficient and sign carried unchanged from the time-domain impulse.

sections.section_title: Handling an Impulse at the Origin with the $0^-$ Convention

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{2\delta(t)\}$ and explain why the $0^-$ limit includes it.

explanation_blocks.text: This is the boundary version of the shifted-impulse rule: identify the form $A\delta(t-T)$ with $A=2$ and $T=0$, then check inclusion using the one-sided limit.
Start from the one-sided Laplace definition.
Substitute $x(t)=2\delta(t)$ into that definition.
Apply sifting at $t=0$, so the value becomes $2e^{-s\cdot 0}=2$. The $0^-$ notation explicitly includes the impulse at the origin; this is not excluded by a strict open boundary at $0$.
So the final result is $2$, and the transform is nonzero because the $0^-$ convention keeps origin impulses in the integration interval.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Shifted Impulses Outside the One-Sided Interval

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{3\delta(t+1)\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The signal still matches the shifted-impulse cue, now with a negative shift: $x(t)=3\delta(t+1)=3\delta(t-(-1))$. The coefficient is $A=3$ and the support point is $T=-1$.
Start from the one-sided definition used in all prior examples.
Substitute the signal into that definition.
Apply sifting at $t=-1$, which gives a candidate $3e^{-s(-1)}=3e^{s}$, but then apply the interval rule first: $T=-1\ge 0$ is false.
Because the impulse support is outside the one-sided interval $[0^-,\infty)$, the weighted integral contributes nothing.
So the final answer is $0$, which distinguishes this edge case from the positive-shift examples where the same rule gives a nonzero exponential result.

entries.lesson_core_move: Invert basic one-sided Laplace-domain transform pairs into causal time-domain signals by recognizing unit-step, exponential, impulse, and shifted-impulse forms under the $0^-$ convention.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Basic Inverse Laplace Transforms

blocks.text: The first move in basic inverse Laplace work is pattern recognition. Read the transform expression as a cue, choose the matching one-sided template, and then write the time-domain signal with the causal support rule.

Use one of these templates: $L^{-1}(1/s)=u(t)$, $L^{-1}(A/(s+a))=A e^{-at}u(t)$, $L^{-1}(A)=A\delta(t)$, and $L^{-1}(A e^{-sT})=A\delta(t-T)$, and in each case attach $u(t)$ only when the expression is one-sided and causal.

If a candidate transform implies a time support that is not one-sided-causal, the template is not applicable in this step. For example, a shifted-impulse form with negative shift is rejected at this stage and must be corrected before inversion.

Apply the one-line checklist before writing the result: identify denominator shift for exponentials, check whether the numerator is constant for an impulse at the origin, and check whether an extra factor $e^{-sT}$ means a delayed impulse rather than an ordinary step or exponential.
Keep notation stable: write $L^{-1}(\cdot)$, $s$-domain symbols like $X(s)$, and time functions like $x(t)$, $u(t)$, and $\delta(t)$ in the same form through later examples and future practice.

sections.section_title: Inverting the Unit-Step Pair

example_content.example_prompt: Find the inverse one-sided transform of $X(s)=1/s$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue in this first inverse example is a pure unit-step form: $X(s)=1/s$. Match this transform directly to the stored base pair rule.
Use the direct substitution rule for this template and write the inverse without adding any scale or shift terms.
Apply the one-sided causal support convention, so the time-domain result is active only for nonnegative time and zero before $t=0$.

sections.section_title: Inverting One-Sided Exponential Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: Find the inverse one-sided transform of $X(s)=4/(s+3)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the denominator is shifted: $X(s)=\frac{4}{s+3}$, so this is an exponential-pair inversion, not a step or impulse pair.
Match the transform to the template $A/(s+a)$ and read off the parameters $A=4$ and $a=3$.
Apply the one-sided support rule and substitute the values: keep $u(t)$ for causality, then attach the mapped exponential decay.
So the inverse transform is $x(t)=4e^{-3t}u(t)$, which keeps the same cue and only adds the denominator-shift parameterization.

sections.section_title: Inverting the Unit-Impulse Pair

example_content.example_prompt: Find the inverse one-sided transform of $X(s)=1$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a pure constant transform: $X(s)=1$. In this sequence, this indicates the unit-impulse template, not a step or exponential form.
Use the direct constant-to-impulse inversion rule and map the constant directly to the origin pulse.
Then preserve one-sided causality by keeping the support at the origin only, with no step factor and no time-shift factor added.
So the final inverse is $x(t)=\delta(t)$, which is the one-sided inverse of a constant $X(s)$.

sections.section_title: Inverting Shifted-Impulse Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: Find the inverse one-sided transform of $X(s)=2e^{-4s}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a delayed-impulse factor: $X(s)=2e^{-4s}$, so this is not a step or exponential pair but the shifted-impulse template.
Match the expression to $A e^{-sT}$ and read $A=2$, $T=4$ as the coefficient and delay.
Substitute $A=2$, $T=4$ and keep the shift positive so the support is at $t=4$ in the one-sided convention.
So the final inverse is $x(t)=2\delta(t-4)$, which is the delayed impulse form under $T\ge 0$ support.

sections.section_title: Choosing Among Basic One-Sided Transform Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: Classify and invert $X(s)=e^{-s}(1+4/(s+2))$ by selecting the best-fit basic one-sided pair.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a delayed product: the outer factor is $e^{-s}$, so classify first by delay before choosing among the internal templates.
Use one-sided delay first: $L^{-1}(e^{-s}F(s))=f(t-1)u(t-1)$, so determine $f(s)$ from the bracketed factor $1+4/(s+2)$.
Inside the bracket, split into $1$ and $4/(s+2)$. The constant maps to $\delta(t)$, and $4/(s+2)$ maps to $4e^{-2t}u(t)$.
Apply the same $t\to t-1$ delay to each component because of the lead $e^{-s}$ factor.
The final inverse is a shifted impulse plus a shifted causal exponential, both with support controlled by $u(t-1)$ where the step-based piece is shown in delayed form.
